analysis.one_liner: Gives House candidates public matching funds for small donations, funded by a surcharge on corporate fines.
analysis.headline: Introduced near the end of the session with 4 cosponsors, the bill was referred to three House committees and never got a hearing or vote; it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a voluntary public financing program for House campaigns. Candidates who collect at least 1,000 small donations totaling $50,000 would get a 6-to-1 federal match on donations of $200 or less, plus extra support before general elections. It would also let three pilot states hand every voting-age resident a $25 voucher to give to a House candidate. The money would come not from taxpayers but from a 4.75% surcharge on corporate criminal fines, civil penalties, and settlements, deposited into a 'Freedom From Influence Fund.' Participating candidates would agree to tight limits: personal spending capped at $50,000, individual contributions capped at $1,000, and no leadership PACs or joint fundraising committees.
analysis.who_benefits: Candidates who can build broad support from small donors — community leaders, teachers, nurses, working people without wealthy networks or personal fortunes — would gain a funding source that matches or beats big-donor money. Small-dollar donors would see each $1-$200 contribution count for seven times its face value. Voucher holders in three pilot states would be able to give without spending their own money.

how_it_helps.text: Participating candidates receive matching payments equal to 600% of qualified small-dollar contributions ($1-$200), up to a cap, with an extra payment worth up to $500,000 before the general election [S2].

To qualify, a candidate must show at least 1,000 individuals contributed and raise at least $50,000 in small-dollar donations, forcing candidates to build a broad base rather than rely on a few large checks [S2].

Three states would run a pilot giving each voting-age resident a $25 'My Voice Voucher' they can allocate in $5 increments to House candidates, letting people give to campaigns without spending their own money [S2].

The financing fund is fed by a 4.75% assessment on corporate criminal fines, civil penalties, settlements, and certain tax penalties, with the bill stating no taxpayer funds may be deposited into it [S2].

Participating candidates may accept at most $1,000 from any individual, may spend only $50,000 of personal or family money, and may not use a leadership PAC or joint fundraising committee during the cycle [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Organizations and corporate officers that pay federal criminal fines, civil penalties, administrative penalties, settlements, or certain tax penalties — overwhelmingly corporations and their executives — would pay a 4.75% surcharge to finance the program. Large individual donors and incumbents who rely on leadership PACs, joint fundraising committees, and unlimited coordinated party spending would face tighter limits if they joined the program, though participation is voluntary.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporations paying federal fines and settlements

drawbacks.text: The 600% federal match means the public pays $6 for every $1 a candidate raises in small donations, and critics would call that a substantial public expenditure even though the bill routes it through a surcharge on fines rather than general tax revenue [S2].
The bill does not touch super PACs or independent expenditures, so outside spending — the fastest-growing channel of big money — would continue unregulated alongside the new program [S2].

The program would not take effect until elections in 2030 at the earliest, the voucher program would run in only 3 states for 2 cycles as a pilot, and both would shut off automatically if the fund runs short [S2].

Candidates who join give up flexibility: they cannot spend freely from personal wealth (capped at $50,000), cannot accept more than $1,000 from any individual, and cannot run joint fundraising operations, which some would argue leaves participating candidates weaker against well-funded opponents who stay out of the program [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: candidates would answer to thousands of small donors instead of a few large ones and wealthy self-funders, at the cost of a new funding stream drawn from fines and penalties on corporate defendants and of rules that constrain participating candidates' own spending. The program's design hedges its costs — no taxpayer appropriations, spending caps, repayment rules for misuse — but it leaves super PACs untouched and wouldn't begin operating until 2030, so its actual effect on who wins House elections would be gradual and partial.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. John Sarbanes introduced the Government by the People Act on May 24, 2024, joined by Reps. Neguse, Clarke of New York, and Pingree [S2].
The bill had 4 cosponsors, all House Democrats [S3].
It was referred to the House Administration, Judiciary, and Ways and Means Committees on the day of introduction; the action history shows no further action [S4].
The bill text incorporates and updates a program from the Government by the People Act of 2021, indicating it was a reintroduction of prior campaign-financing legislation [S2].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, with the bill still in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent officeholders and the large donors, joint fundraising operations, and leadership PACs that finance them keep the existing campaign money system, and corporate defendants avoid the 4.75% surcharge on fines and settlements. Candidates who depend on small donors gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and it died in committee under the Republican House majority without any roll call on it.

industries.industry: Large political donors, joint fundraising committees, and leadership PACs
industries.note: Participating candidates could accept no more than $1,000 per donor, could not run joint fundraising committees or leadership PACs, and party committees could only spend unlimited coordinated money if it came from small-dollar accounts — shrinking the channels through which concentrated money reaches House campaigns. Donors' influence over candidates would diminish relative to thousands of small contributors.

industries.industry: Corporate defendants paying federal fines, penalties, and settlements
industries.note: A 4.75% surcharge on criminal fines, civil and administrative penalties, settlements, and certain tax penalties would finance the campaign fund. These surcharges fall almost entirely on corporations and their officers, so the entities that face federal enforcement would pay for cleaner elections.

industries.industry: Small-dollar political donors and non-wealthy House candidates
industries.note: A $1-$200 donation would generate a 600% federal match, and a $25 voucher pilot would let voting-age residents give without spending their own money. This lowers the barrier to candidacy for people without personal wealth or wealthy networks.

New public money flowing to participating candidates would expand total campaign spending on services and advertising, though candidates could use the funds only for direct payments for authorized campaign goods and services, not legal defense or fines.
